issues.legal_issue: A High Court may set aside an acquittal in revision when the acquittal rests on compounding an offence that cannot legally be compounded.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after the complainant said he did not wish to proceed and the court treated the offences as compounded.
One of the charged offences was not compoundable, with or without court permission.
issues.conclusion: The High Court rightly set aside the acquittal and directed the trial to proceed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 345(7) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an offence may be compounded only as provided by that section. An acquittal based on compounding that is invalid in law may be set aside in revision, as held in K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 412.

predicates.criminal_revision_of_acquittal: A reviewing court considers a criminal revision against a trial court's acquittal.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_compounding: The trial court acquitted the accused because it treated the offence or offences as compounded.
predicates.at_least_one_offence_not_legally_compoun: At least one offence underlying the acquittal could not legally be compounded.

issues.definition: When a criminal revision concerns an acquittal based on compounding and at least one offence could not legally be compounded, the acquittal is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may exercise criminal revisional jurisdiction on its own initiative when information from any source makes it consider a subordinate court's order fit for revision.
material_facts: The trial magistrate sent papers to the High Court for appropriate action after the complainant alleged that the accused had failed to fulfil an undertaking.
The High Court gave the accused notice to show cause why the acquittal should not be set aside, then set it aside in revision on its own initiative.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's exercise of revisional power on its own initiative involved no procedural irregularity.
issues.legal_principle: The opening words of section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, permit the High Court to exercise revisional jurisdiction when proceedings come to its knowledge, including on its own initiative. State of Kerala v. Narayani Amma Kamala Devi, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 943, establishes that information from any source is sufficient if it makes the High Court consider the subordinate court's order fit for revision.

predicates.criminal_revision_proceeding: The matter before the High Court is a criminal revision concerning an order of a subordinate court.
predicates.information_reaches_high_court: Information about the subordinate court's order reaches the High Court from any source.
predicates.information_indicates_order_fit_for_revi: The information makes the High Court consider the subordinate court's order fit for revisional review.

issues.definition: When information reaching the High Court in a criminal revision makes it consider a subordinate court's order fit for review, the High Court may validly act on its own initiative.

issues.legal_issue: An indivisible permission to compound multiple offences cannot be upheld in part when one of those offences cannot legally be compounded.
material_facts: The acquittal concerned charges under two offences, one of which could be compounded only with court permission and the other of which could not be compounded.
No order granting permission to compound the compoundable offence was produced, and the court considered the possibility of permission having been granted.
The permission, if granted, was indivisible and related to both offences; the court could not determine that permission would have been granted for only the compoundable offence.
issues.conclusion: The permission was invalid in its entirety and could not be severed to preserve the acquittal for the compoundable offence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code permitted compounding only with the court's permission, while the offence under section 13 of the Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963, was not compoundable. Because the permission was indivisible and covered both offences, it could not be severed and upheld for only one. Section 345(7) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, permits compounding only as provided by that section.

predicates.criminal_revision_of_acquittal: A reviewing court considers a criminal revision against an acquittal based on compounding.
predicates.single_indivisible_permission_for_multip: The permission to compound was one indivisible permission covering multiple offences.
predicates.at_least_one_offence_not_legally_compoun: At least one offence covered by the permission could not legally be compounded.

issues.definition: When an acquittal is reviewed in criminal revision and a single indivisible permission covered multiple offences, one of which could not legally be compounded, the entire permission is invalid.
